title: Frog it or leave it?
standfirst: There is a project in your basket that you keep picking up and putting down again. Six questions, then a straight answer — frog it, fix it, or leave it alone.
intro: Answer honestly — the useless version of this quiz is the one you fill in as the person you wish you were.
teaser: Six questions for the project you keep picking up and putting down again, and one straight answer at the end — frog it, fix it, or leave it alone.
calloutTeaser: Six questions about the project currently sulking in your basket, and one honest answer at the end.
tileCaption: Frog it · Fix it · Leave it
resultFootnote: A quiz cannot see your fabric. If the answer and your gut disagree, your gut has more information — put the project in a bag for a week and ask again.
metaDescription: Six questions about the project you keep putting down, and one straight answer: frog it, fix it, or leave it alone.

outcomes.name: Fix it.
outcomes.line: The problem is smaller than your feelings about it.
outcomes.body: What is wrong with this project is local — one row, one motif, one seam — and everything around it is fine. Frogging the whole thing to fix a patch is the expensive option, and the version of you who finishes it this month will not remember the repair.
steps: Find the last row you are happy with and mark it with a locking marker before you touch anything.
Frog back to that row only. Wind as you go, even for twenty stitches.
If the fix needs a new join, join at a seam or an edge, never mid-row on a visible panel.
Then keep going the same day. A project put down straight after a repair rarely gets picked back up.

outcomes.name: Frog it.
outcomes.line: The yarn deserves a second try. So do you.
outcomes.body: This is not going to become something you use, and every hour you spend on it is an hour the yarn is not being something else. Frogging is not failure — it is the only craft where you get the whole material back.
steps: Check the yarn first: fuzzy mohair, alpaca halo, or a delicate single ply may not survive. Frog ten rows as a test before committing.
Wind as you unravel — a swift and winder if you have them, a centre-pull ball by hand if not.
Skein it loosely, soak it lukewarm, hang it to dry with no weight. That is what takes the old stitch memory out.
Write down what actually went wrong before you cast on again, or you will do it a second time.

outcomes.name: Leave it alone.
outcomes.line: Nothing is wrong with it. Something is wrong with today.
outcomes.body: By your own answers this is a project you would use and a fabric you like. What you have is boredom, or the middle third, which feels identical to boredom and is not. Do not take a permanent decision in a temporary mood.
steps: Put it in a bag, out of sight, and set a date two weeks out.
Start something small and fast in the meantime — the point is to finish something, anything.
On the date, look at it in daylight before you look at the pattern.
If it still bores you then, reread this quiz. The answer will have changed and that answer is trustworthy.

questions.q: What is actually wrong with it?
questions.note: The first honest sentence, not the polite one.

options.label: The gauge or the size is off
options.sub: It will not fit, or the fabric came out a different size than the pattern promised

options.label: There is one visible mistake a few rows back
options.sub: A missed increase, a wrong stitch, a twisted round

options.label: I have gone off the colour or the yarn
options.sub: It is well made. I just do not like looking at it

options.label: Nothing, really. I am just bored of it
options.sub: It is fine. I have simply stopped wanting to work on it

questions.q: How far into the project are you?
questions.note: Sunk cost is real, but it is not always the deciding factor.

options.label: The first few rows
options.sub: Almost nothing to lose

options.label: Roughly a third of the way
options.sub: Enough to hurt, not enough to be nearly done

options.label: Nearly finished
options.sub: Sleeves, edging, or seams left

options.label: Finished, blocked, and unworn
options.sub: It exists. It just lives in a drawer

questions.q: Would you wear or use it exactly as it is now?
questions.note: As it is. Not as it would be after the imaginary fix.

options.label: Yes, happily
options.sub: Out of the house, without thinking about it

options.label: Only at home
options.sub: It is comfortable and I do not mind the flaws

options.label: No
options.sub: I would find a reason not to, every time

questions.note: This decides whether frogging is even possible — halo and fragile plies do not always survive.

options.label: Smooth and tightly spun
options.sub: Wool, cotton, linen, most superwash — frogs cleanly

options.label: Fluffy — mohair, brushed alpaca, a real halo
options.sub: The fibres grip each other and fight back

options.label: Delicate — a fine single ply, or already fraying
options.sub: It has broken on me before

options.label: No idea, the label is long gone
options.sub: Test it on ten rows before you decide

questions.q: Is the problem in one place, or in the whole fabric?
questions.note: Local problems get repaired. Structural ones do not.

options.label: One row, one motif, one spot
options.sub: I could point at it

options.label: A whole section — the yoke, a sleeve, a seam line
options.sub: It would mean redoing a real chunk

options.label: The fabric itself is wrong
options.sub: Stiff, floppy, dense, holey — the stitch and the yarn do not suit each other

questions.q: And when you pick it up, honestly, what do you feel?
questions.note: Last question. This one carries the most weight, because it is the one you already knew.

options.label: Dread
options.sub: I move it off the chair and do something else

options.label: Irritation at one specific bit
options.sub: Everything else is fine and I know exactly where I am annoyed

options.label: Fondness
options.sub: I like it. I just have not been in the mood
